When to Use -ed and -ing Adjectives

Adjectives which are formed from Infinitive verb forms can have two types of endings: -ed and -ing.
Adjectives ending in -ed describe how someone feels.
Adjectives ending in -ing describe how something or someone is, or how a situation makes someone feel.

Adjectives ending in -ed can only be used to describe feelings or emotions. They describe how a person feels. They cannot be used to describe an object or situation.
Example: Sir Edmund Hillary was fascinated by the idea of climbing Mt Everest.

Adjectives ending in -ing can be used either with a person or a situation. They describe the characteristics of a person or a situation. They also describe how a situation makes you feel.
Example: Sir Edmund Hillary found the idea of climbing Mt Everest fascinating.

Compare the differences:
  • Sir Hillary is fascinated. (he feels fascinated)
  • Sir Hillary is fascinating. (he is a fascinating person).
  • Climbing Mt Everest is a fascinating challenge. (It causes people to feel fascinated)
You cannot say Mt Everest is fascinated, since it is not a person.

Simple Past Passive to Report Events
You can use the passive voice when you want to report events that happened in the past in a general way.

Most of spoken English uses active speech. When you use an active sentence to report an event, the subject is the focus of the sentence.
Example:
  • Journalists (subject) reported a sharp increase in mountain climbing as a recreational activity (object).

A passive sentence puts the emphasis on the object of the active sentence. When you use a passive sentence to report an event, the object of the active sentence now becomes the subject and focus of the passive sentence.
Example:
  • A sharp increase in mountain climbing as a recreational activity (subject) was reported by many journalists (object).

You can use the Simple Past passive form to report events in an impersonal way. The subject is not specific, but general.
Example:
  • It was said that mountain climbing was only practiced by seasoned explorers, but that has changed over the years.
You make the passive form of a verb by using tenses of the be verb followed by the past participle.

You use the structure:
subject + Simple Past passive reporting verb + To-Infinitive (Perfect or Perfect Continuous tense)

images.text:
For most of modern history, Mount Everest was said to be unclimbable. At 8,848 metres, it was thought to be too high, dangerous, and terrifying to climb. It was first suggested to be possible in 1885 in a book entitled Above the Snow Line. The author, Clinton Thomas Dent, was convinced that it could be achieved. The feat wouldn't be successfully accomplished, however, for another 50-plus years.
After several failed expeditions, it was a New Zealander, Edmund Hillary, and a Nepali sherpa, Tenzing Norgay, who were credited with first reaching the peak.
For many years, Hillary and Norgay were reported to have summited together, but it was later confirmed that the New Zealander had been the first to set foot at the top.

Mountain climbing used to be an activity only done by explorers like Hillary and Norgay, but over time it has become a mainstream sport. That being said, this challenging sport is certainly not for the timid or careless. To be a successful mountaineer, a person needs to be patient. It is very easy to become frustrated if progress is slow or weather conditions force a change of plan.
Because it is such a frustrating activity, climbers must be resourceful. They must use their brains as well as their bodies to reach the top of the mountain. Lastly, alpinists must be well-equipped with the appropriate gear, including ropes and pitons.

Each mountain ascent presents new challenges and a climber has to be prepared for different mountain conditions and environmental factors. If the mountain is steep and icy, climbers have to take extra precaution. They must plan their climbs well and calculate each step.
Mountain climbing, like most exciting sports, can be dangerous. But for thrill-seekers, the rush of summiting outweighs the fear.
